posts.title: BMS Architecture
posts.heading: What an EV Battery Recall Teaches Us About BMS Architecture
posts.subheading: A memory-arbitration race between two ICs, and three things it should change about how you scope BMS and firmware work.
posts.description: A major automaker's shared EV platform recalled roughly 21,000 vehicles for a defect inside the battery control unit.
posts.richBody:
## The Root Cause

1. Two ICs on the board could write to the same memory address at the same time.
2. One overwrites the other mid-write.
3. The battery ECU faults.
4. **The vehicle loses drive power on the road.**

## This Isn't Just a "Software Bug"

This isn't a software bug in the vague sense marketing teams use. It's a **concurrency and memory-arbitration failure** — the kind unit tests miss, that passes hardware validation, and only shows up when two independent silicon paths race for the same register under real-world timing.

## OTA and Field Remediation

The manufacturer could fix this with an OTA update through the OBD-II port. Most hardware startups can't.

If your BMS or IoT node doesn't have OTA and a dual-bank bootloader from day one, the same class of bug means a truck roll or a physical recall — not a push notification.

## Three Things This Should Change About How You Scope BMS/Firmware Work

### 01 · Shared memory access

Shared memory access between any two ICs (companion chip, fuel gauge, processor) needs explicit arbitration — mutex, semaphore, or a single owner — documented in the architecture review, not discovered in the field.

### 02 · OTA & rollback

OTA and rollback capability isn't a "phase 2" feature. It's what turns a $500-per-vehicle recall into a $0 remote patch.

### 03 · End-to-end ownership

When your chip vendor, RTOS integrator, and mechanical/enclosure team are three different vendors, concurrency bugs like this hide in the handoffs — nobody owns the full data path end to end.

## Our Approach

We build BMS and embedded systems as one team — hardware, firmware, and infrastructure under one roof — specifically so races like this get caught in architecture review, not in a regulatory filing.

## Scope a BMS or IoT product?

If you're scoping a BMS or IoT product and want a second set of eyes on your memory/concurrency architecture before it ships, book a scoping call.

posts.title: Power Electronics
posts.heading: Dual-Channel Smart Charger: Power and Firmware, Designed Together
posts.subheading: Why the control loop and the converter topology were decided in the same room.
posts.richBody:
The converter topology and the control loop shape one another. We considered them together from the first architecture decisions, then tested the complete system against the product's real operating conditions.

That early collaboration helped align power behavior, protection, and firmware before the design moved into validation.

posts.title: Industrial IoT
posts.heading: BLE Mesh + RS485: Retrofitting Energy Meters Without Rewiring
posts.subheading: A mesh-networked node that speaks Modbus downstream and BLE Mesh upstream.
posts.description: A mesh-networked node that speaks Modbus downstream and BLE Mesh upstream.
posts.richBody:
Retrofitting installed energy meters can avoid costly rewiring. This node connects existing Modbus equipment over RS485 and carries data upstream over BLE Mesh.

The design keeps the field connection familiar while adding a practical path for connected monitoring.

posts.title: Apps & Cloud
posts.heading: Edge Compute Gateway: OTA Across a Distributed Fleet
posts.subheading: Dual-bank updates, signed images, and automatic rollback for smart-infrastructure deployments.
posts.description: Dual-bank updates, signed images, and automatic rollback for smart-infrastructure deployments.
posts.richBody:
Fleet updates need to be secure, observable, and recoverable. This gateway uses signed images, a dual-bank update path, and automatic rollback so a failed update does not strand a deployed device.

The deployment plan treats fleet management as part of the product architecture, rather than a service to bolt on later.

posts.title: Hardware & PCB
posts.heading: Where Board Respins Actually Come From
posts.subheading: Most respins trace back to decisions made before layout started.
posts.description: Most respins trace back to decisions made before layout started. Here's where we look first on every new board.
posts.richBody:
Board respins often begin with choices made before the first trace is routed: unclear requirements, late component selection, untested interfaces, and layout constraints discovered too late.

A short architecture review and focused early prototypes can surface these risks while changes are still inexpensive.

posts.title: Validation
posts.heading: EMC Pre-Compliance Before You Book the Lab
posts.subheading: The bench checks that catch radiation and immunity issues early.
posts.description: The bench checks that catch radiation and immunity issues early, while fixes are still a layout change and not a redesign.
posts.richBody:
Pre-compliance testing gives the team an opportunity to find emissions and immunity issues before formal certification. A focused bench setup and a repeatable test plan help connect a failure to its likely source.

Finding a layout issue before a certification booking can save both schedule and redesign effort.

posts.title: Firmware
posts.heading: Choosing an RTOS for Battery-Powered Products
posts.subheading: Scheduling, power states, and update paths — how the RTOS decision shapes battery life long before the enclosure is closed.
posts.description: Scheduling, power states, and update paths — how the RTOS decision shapes battery life long before the enclosure is closed.
posts.richBody:
An RTOS influences more than task scheduling. Its power-management model, drivers, update support, and debugging tools all affect the product lifecycle.

Compare candidates against concrete application requirements and validate the most important power states on representative hardware.
